messages.subject: ar1 with panel data
messages.body_plain:
Does INLA's ar(1) effect work correctly when the data
contains multiple instances of each time variable? There's
a discussion in Blangiardo+Cameletti which suggests that
it should (in the context of the rw(1) model, not ar(1))
but I'm not sure.

Consider the example in the ar1.pdf write-up. Here we
have a sample of 100 observations. Supose now that we
stack copies of the dataset, so that we work with 200 and
then 300 observations.  I'd expect that the resulting
estimates would be similar, but what I get is
(for the means, sd's in parens):

Num. Obs.   Intercept       prec(z)        rho
True                        10.00         0.80
100       .1493 (.11)   6.67 (2.09    0.70 (.11)
200           .1251 (.10)   4.54 (1.03)   0.55 (.11)
300           .1129 (.09)   3.93 (0.79)   0.48 (.11)

To me it looks as if the larger the sample size,
the further away from the true values the estimates
become. Is this what experts would expect? Maybe
my intuitions are just wrong. Or am
I doing something wrong, and there's something else
I need to do in order to correctly implement an ar(1)
random effects structure when I have a panel dataset?

[PS- the writeup for rw(1) says that it has an example
illustrating the use of the values parameter. Best I
can see, it doesn't].

Thanks for any help/advice!

messages.body_plain:
Hi

yes, the problem is deep. the issue is that student-t is not log-
concave, and the question is what to do if the local hessian for the
log student-t (like for one observation) has the wrong sign. its like
getting variance < 0, so the contribution for the student-t observation
will locally inflate the variance, not reducing it.

its possible to truncate this at 0, meaning that if the hessian has the
wrong sign, set it to zero. you can do this using

control.inla = list(cmin = 0)

where the default value is -Inf which means do nothing.  its unclear
what is the better thing to do, beyond the obvious, which comes with a
higher cost.

to be honest, I do not like the student-t anymore ;-)

H

messages.subject: How does INLA sample from implicit GMRFs?
messages.subject_clean: How does INLA sample from implicit GMRFs?
messages.body_plain:
The second order random walk (RW2) has a precision matrix of rank n-2 which leads to ambiguities with sampling realisations of the process, as outlined in Rue&Held (2005, ch. 3.2). They provide Algorithm 3.1 to sample from GMRFs with rank deficient precision matrices, but INLA internally seems to do something differently.

Here is my implementation of Algorithm 3.1 or RH05:

n = 250
# Precision matrix of RW2 with kappa=1; RH05, eq. 3.40
Q = Matrix::bandSparse(n=n, k=0:2, sym=TRUE, diag=list(c(1,5,rep(6,n-4),5,1), c(-2,rep(-4,n-3),-2), rep(1, n-2)))
# eigen decomposition
Qeig = eigen(Q)
# sample y iid Normal with precisions equal to the nonzero eigenvalues of Q
y = rnorm(n-2, 0, 1/sqrt(Qeig$values[1:(n-2)]))
# project y onto eigenvectors of Q; x is a "sample" of an RW2
x = drop(Qeig$vectors[, 1:(n-2)] %*% y)

We can verify the algorithm by checking that the second order difference `diff(diff(x))` is approximately iid Normal(0,1). Sampling many realisations like this produces the following plot. There are obvious artifacts, which I think are due to the implicit constraint that mean and slope are exactly zero.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-uA6JgbcwFY8/WhdFL_WPc-I/AAAAAAAAAAM/rN50AZTtxqYEPvXlxrpr_2zYX_QAR3SOQCLcBGAs/s1600/rw2-custom-2-1.png>

With R-INLA, realisations of RW2 can be generated by setting all data to NA, thus sampling from the prior:

result = inla(data=data.frame(i=1:n, y=NA), formula = y ~ -1 + f(i, model='rw2', hyper=list(theta=list(initial=0, fixed=TRUE))), family='gaussian', control.family=list(hyper=list(theta=list(initial=20, fixed=TRUE))), control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
samples = inla.posterior.sample(n=100, result=result)
# ... and then extracting samples[[1 ... 100]]$latent[i:1 ... i:250]

`diff(diff(x))` behaves as expected. The generated samples look much "nicer". What does INLA do internally to avoid the artifacts I got in the first plot?

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-11TPLcfyw90/WhdJLcLJx5I/AAAAAAAAAAY/sdUTgZsnrfEvUzJIe0emYeYymRoNuow5wCLcBGAs/s1600/rw2-inla-1.png>

Hi,

first of all, the effect you see in the first plot is not really an "artefact"; it's what's left
after removing the mean and linear slope from the process. To first order, that's
roughly a quadratic function for a 'rw2' process, and that's exactly what shows up
in the plot.  When used in a model, any sufficiently informative data will remove
the rank deficiency, so even without the constraints, the posterior distribution is
well defined.  Constraints are however often imposed to help with identifiability
and structure the model; you can't have two covariate effects follow unconstrained
rw2 models, since that leads to non-identifiable intercepts. Imposing a mean-zero
constraint on each of them, and instead having an explicit intercept term in the
model is identifiable (if the covariates are not themselves confounded).

While the documentation for 'rw2' does say that it is rank deficient of
order 2 (arbitrary mean and slope), it _also_ says that the default value
of 'constr' is TRUE, which means that it does impose a sum-to-zero
constraint (but not slope = zero).
This means that when comparing it to the explicit zero mean _and_ zero slope
version should be expected to differ.

However, without the zero-slope constraint, the model should exhibit a
_different_ type of "artefact", which your second, inla, version does not.
I suspect this is due to your code trying to extract information about the
prior model, and that some of the numerical constructs used internally
really only make sense when there is some actual data involved. It looks
like the effect is the same as if you had entered independent N(0,sigma^2)
variables as observations, for some large value of sigma^2, which should
have the effect of suppressing the slope and curvature of the process, as
exhibited in your figure.

This should normally have only a negligible effect on the _posterior_
distributions that R-INLA is designed to compute, but perhaps some of these
numerical necessities need to be made clearer so that effects on edge cases
like this (trying to compute a prior) become better known.

PS. I _may_ have misdiagnosed the issue...

Finn

messages.body_plain:
A safer way to compare your own calculations with inla for this case
would be to impose constraints on say, the first and last element of
the process, setting them to zero. Either the same constraint simulation
technique can be used for those constraints, or one can use the fact that
the conditional precision is the submatrix obtained by deleting the first
and last rows&columns.

In inla, you'd then set f(..., constr=FALSE) to remove the sum-to-zero
constraint, but then have two observations for the first and last element
equal to zero, with observation variance precision very large, e.g. 1e10.

Then you should hopefully get the same "second order Brownian bridge
type behaviour from your standalone computations as those produced
by inla.

Finn

Maybe your suggestion of specifying the linear constraints solves the problem?

messages.body_plain:
What you see is a basic consequence of dealing with singular/intrinsic models. They are numerically ill-defined in the prior, and are therefore heavily dependent on the precise method used for calculations. The most important step is to choose the techniques such that the _posteriors_ distributions are correct. (Some of those, such as imposing both mean and slope zero constraints also give stable interpretations on the prior side of things; others do not.) Or to not use an intrinsic model.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
The problem is that the different limiting arguments give rise to different behaviour away from the actual limit, and for the rw2 case there are more possible choices than for rw1. Comparing the appearance under one argument with the appearance under another and observing different behaviour doesn’t mean that either of them is necessarily _wrong_. In this case it means that the problem is fundamentally ill-posed, and that researcher choices matter. Imposing constraints _changes_ the model in one way. Adding epsilon to the precision diagonal _changes_ the model in a different way. For rw2 in inla without any data, the implementation results in a hybrid. One constraint, and epsilon added to the diagonal, resulting in a third version of the model.
All three versions are related to the actual intrinsic model in different ways, and must be interpreted in light of those specific choices.

Finn

messages.subject: Average Marginal Effect (AME)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Using a simple model in INLA I can estimate the Average Marginal Effect (AME - average over empirical range of observed data) easily for a binary covariate x1=0,1.  (The continuous case is slightly more complicated). I simply create two copies of the original data, set the predicted outcome to NA, and set x1 to 0 in the first predicted dataset and x1 to 1 in the second.

I then use inla.predicted.sample as follows and get results that match up well when using the "margins" command (frequentist):

-------------------------------------------------------
require(margins)
require(INLA)

## simulation ##

set.seed(1)
N <- 1000
x1 <- sample(c(0,1),N,rep=T)
x2 <- rnorm(N)
mu <- 0.1 + 1.0*x1 + 0.5*x2 + 0.2*x1*x2
p <- plogis(mu)
y <- rbinom(N,1,prob=p)
dat <- data.frame(x1,x2,y)

## frequentist way

mod.glm <- glm(y ~ x1*x2,data=dat,family="binomial")
print( summary(margins(mod.glm)), digits=3)

## Bayesian way

pred.0 <- dat; pred.0$x1 <- 0; pred.0$y <- NA
pred.1 <- dat; pred.1$x1 <- 1; pred.1$y <- NA
dat.pred <- rbind(dat,pred.0,pred.1)

require(INLA)
mod.inla <- inla(y ~ x1*x2,family="binomial",data=dat.pred,
                 control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
                 control.predictor=list(link=1),
                 )
M <- 1000
samp <- inla.posterior.sample(M,mod.inla)
latents <- t(sapply(samp,function(x) x$latent[,1]))
preds <- plogis(latents)[,which(is.na <http://is.na>(dat.pred$y))]

## calculate ame
p0 <- preds[,1:N]
p1 <- preds[,N + 1:N]
ame <- rowMeans(p1-p0)
print( quantile(ame,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975)), digits=3)

## relative risks - hard to get from frequentist logistic models
rr.1.0 <- rowMeans(p1/p0)
quantile(rr.2.1,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))

-----------------------------------------

I'm curious if this is perhaps a slow/inefficient way to do this. In particular, is there a way to do it without using inla.posterior.sample?

Thanks,

John

p1. If you are willing to ignore their posterior dependence, you can

predictors for p0 and p1, are joint Gaussian, you can extract (from
defining appropriate linear combinations) the correlation between these
two, and then you have the Gaussian copula. Then you can just sample
from a bivariate normal or do integration in 2d.

messages.body_plain:
How about considering the "An alternative limit argument for the first-order IGRMF" proposed just before section 3.4 in the GMRF book? It suggests to consider add a small value to the diagonal. I tried using inla.qsample() as follows:
n <- 250
Q <- crossprod(diff(Diagonal(n), diff=2))
x <- inla.qsample(100, Q+Diagonal(n,1e-5))
plot.ts(x[,1], ylim=range(x))
for (j in 1:100)
    lines(x[,j], col=rgb(j/100, 1-abs(j-50)/50, 1-j/100))

Considering the sum-to-zero constraint

xc <- inla.qsample(100, Q+Diagonal(n,1e-5),
                   constr=list(A=matrix(1,1,n), e=0))
plot.ts(xc[,1], ylim=range(xc))
for (j in 1:100)
    lines(xc[,j], col=rgb(j/100, 1-abs(j-50)/50, 1-j/100))

Elias

> > the rank deficiency, so even without the constraints, the posterior distribution is
> > well defined.  Constraints are however often imposed to help with identifiability
> > and structure the model; you can't have two covariate effects follow unconstrained
> > rw2 models, since that leads to non-identifiable intercepts. Imposing a mean-zero

messages.subject_clean: Non-Gaussian random effects for frailty models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am considering the implementation of Gamma random effects for frailty survival models in INLA using the rgeneric. My approach would be to set the precision of the GMRF to a large value and then put a Gamma prior on the means of the GMRF. Then I could also have some priors on the parameters of the Gamma distribution (if needed), i.e, random effects u would be defined as follows:

(1) u|mu, prec ~ GMRF(mu, prec = large value)
(2) u_i|a, b  ~ Gamma (a, b)
(3) a|hyper.a ~ Prior()
(4) b|hyper.b  ~ Prior()

Here, (1) would be in the part of the GMRF, with a diagonal matrix with very large values in the diagonal. (2) to (3) would be in the log.prior() function. Hyperparameters to be reported by INLA would be (a, b, hyper.a, hyper.b)

Do you think that this would work? Note that setting the precision of the GMRF to a large value is a trick to avoid the 'middle layer' of the GMRF. What I am not sure about is how INLA will handle this formulation and if it will have some side effects...

Best,

Virgilio

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am implementing a spatio-temporal model for geostatistical data involving a response variable and two covariates which are spatially misaligned.
One of the covariates is assumed to vary in time only, and the other varies in space only. Plus, there is an additional categorical spatial covariate.

I am simulating the response with measurement error and linear predictor which is the sum of the covariates and an additional space-time residual u which can be drawn from iid, spatially dependent (iid in time) or spatio-temporal (spatially structured component + temporally structured component, no space-time interaction).
This constitues an extension of the example in chapter 8.1 of the Blangiardo and Cameletti book.

The issue is that, when the residual u term is assumed not to vary in time, the current inla call on simulated data produces unexpected predicted values that look identical in all the time points (731 days) and only differ in space.
However, the fitted values look as expected for the model in which the error term is spatio-temporal, as if the whole temporal variability was expressed by this term.

I can't figure out what I am doing wrong in the data simulation, assuming the model specification is correct.

I attach the script which contains a short description of the data and the model, the data simulation, and the inla steps.

Thank you for any suggestion.

Best,

Chiara

from your text description it sounds like you intended to have at
least one spatio-temporal model component x(s,t), but in your code all

processes.
Your inla.spde.make.index and inla.spde.make.A calls however make use
of n.group, which indicates that you really did intend to have some
x(s,t) components, but then you need to do

  f(field, model=spde, group=field.group, control.group=list(model="ar1", ...))

and not

  f(field, model=spde) + f(field.group, model="ar1")

The second version (which is what you have in your code) makes a
x1(s)+x2(t) model, and the first version (which I think is what you
intended) gives x(s,t).

Finn
